title: Work close
hook: sixty days on work, and the last move: finish, look, rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, five answers side by side: curse, calling, offering, duty, livelihood. Your line was the part matters more than the applause. Which one fit your work this week? Today, we close the question. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

A carpenter sets down the plane, runs a palm along the tabletop, and steps back. Not to start the next job. Just to look. That small pause, between the last stroke and the next thing, is where this whole stretch on work ends. When this stretch began, we met a garden that needed tending. Since then: a craftsman filled with spirit, a tentmaker, a farmer Guru, a woodworker who fasted before he carved, a Chan master who wouldn't eat on a day he didn't work. This week alone, a harvest, a written answer to what your work really is, service, attention, and five different answers. Today, the last move. Finish. Look. Rest.
screen: `STEP BACK AND LOOK.` → `SIXTY DAYS ON WORK.` → `FINISH. LOOK. REST.`

segments.voice: First, finishing. Back on day eight hundred eighty-six, Rabbi Tarfon said it isn't yours to finish the work, nor are you free to stop. That's true of the big work: justice, a family, a life. But inside the big work are small things that can be finished. A drawer. A letter. A report. Finishing one is its own kind of practice. Second, looking. Again and again in the creation story, Genesis pauses to look. And at the end of the sixth day, the King James says: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." The work isn't over until someone looks at it. Not to find the flaw. To see it. Third, rest. The next verses don't start a new project. "And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made." In that story, rest isn't what's left when the work runs out. It's part of the shape. Fourth, the whole block in one line. The traditions gave very different answers about what work is. But across the texts we read, the same rhythm kept showing up: do the work with care, then stop. The Benedictine hours, the Sabbath, Friday prayers, the observance days. Work well, then rest. Ecclesiastes says there's a season for everything, "and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Work had its season on this path. Tomorrow a new question begins.
screen: `FINISH ONE SMALL THING.` · `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.` · `HE RESTED ON THE SEVENTH DAY.` · `WORK WELL, THEN STOP.` · then, large: `WORK WELL, THEN REST.`

segments.voice: Before the bell, choose one small thing you can finish today. Small enough to actually finish: one email, one shelf, one form, one mended button. Now sit, and let the breath slow. See yourself doing it with care, from the first step to the last. Then see yourself stepping back, the way the carpenter did, and simply looking at it. No checking for mistakes. Just looking. Then let your hands rest in your lap. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own tradition's words for the work of these weeks. The bell holds the time.
Sabbath. The end of sixty days on work: finish something, look at it, and rest. Today's word.
Your line: work well, then rest. Today, finish the one thing you chose, step back and look at it for a moment, and then stop for real. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Several traditions pair work with set times of rest: the Jewish Sabbath, Christian Sunday rest, Friday congregational prayer in Islam, monastic hours of prayer, and Buddhist observance days.

notes: Block D close and week-end day (932–938). 'Sixty days' is the block's span in the outline (days 879–938).

The hook names earlier days' figures by their outline titles (Genesis 2:15, Bezalel, Paul the tentmaker, Guru Nanak at Kartarpur, Woodworker Qing, Baizhang). Confirm they match what those scripts taught.
Pirkei Avot 2:16 (Rabbi Tarfon) paraphrased; numbering differs between editions (2:16 or 2:21).
'Across the texts we read, the same rhythm kept showing up' refers only to the block's own days (Benedict, Sabbath, the stopping days of day 914), not to all traditions.

Editor pass: 'at the end of each day of creation' corrected (the KJV has no 'God saw that it was good' on the second day) to 'again and again'; 'sixty days ago we started with a garden' changed to 'when this stretch began', since the garden was day 880, not the block's first day.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): 'at the end of the sixth' made 'at the end of the sixth day' (the bare 'sixth' was unclear after 'again and again'). Genesis 1:31, 2:2 and Ecclesiastes 3:1 KJV checked exact. 'Friday prayers' as a rest rhythm is loose (Qur'an 62:9–10 pauses trade for prayer, not a day of rest); Keeper may prefer 'Friday prayer, a pause in trade'.
